summary: Carmustine (BCNU) is a lipophilic nitrosourea alkylating agent that crosses the blood-brain barrier, used as palliative therapy for brain tumors, multiple myeloma, and relapsed/refractory Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas. It carries boxed warnings for cumulative, delayed myelosuppression and dose-related pulmonary toxicity. Doses are given no more often than every 6 weeks and adjusted to hematologic nadirs.
indications: Brain tumors (glioblastoma, brainstem glioma, medulloblastoma, astrocytoma, ependymoma, metastatic brain tumors) as a single agent or in combination
Multiple myeloma in combination with prednisone
Relapsed or refractory Hodgkin's lymphoma in combination with other approved drugs
Relapsed or refractory non-Hodgkin's lymphomas in combination with other approved drugs

admin: Administer reconstituted solution only as a slow IV infusion over at least 2 hours
Do not repeat dosing more frequently than every 6 weeks
Monitor the infusion site closely - extravasation causes local injury
Handle as a hazardous cytotoxic drug; protect from contact with skin
moa: The mechanism is not fully understood. Carmustine alkylates and cross-links DNA and RNA, interfering with replication and transcription, and is not cross-resistant with other alkylators. As a nitrosourea it may also inhibit key enzymatic processes by carbamoylation of amino acids in proteins. Its high lipophilicity allows penetration of the blood-brain barrier.

absolute: Previous hypersensitivity to carmustine or its components
relative: Pre-existing or drug-induced bone marrow suppression

preg: Can cause fetal harm based on mechanism and animal data. Advise females of reproductive potential of the risk to a fetus and to avoid pregnancy during treatment. Verify pregnancy status before starting.
lact: Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in a breastfed infant, advise women not to breastfeed during treatment with carmustine.
renal: Dose reduction is recommended in renal impairment; monitor renal function during therapy.
hepatic: Dose reduction is recommended in hepatic impairment; monitor liver function tests during therapy.

major: Other myelosuppressive chemotherapy or radiation (additive marrow suppression)
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; may worsen nausea and hepatic burden
interactions.diagnostics: May increase liver enzymes, bilirubin, BUN and creatinine; lowers blood counts

serious: Severe, cumulative and delayed bone marrow suppression
emergency: Acute respiratory failure from pulmonary toxicity

monitoring: Complete blood count weekly for at least 6 weeks after each dose
Pulmonary function tests at baseline and periodically (cumulative dose >1400 mg/m2 high risk)
Cumulative lifetime dose and signs of delayed pulmonary toxicity (which may occur years later)
counsel: This is a chemotherapy drug given by slow IV infusion; report breathing difficulty, cough, fever, bleeding or bruising promptly
Nausea and flushing during/after infusion are common
Avoid pregnancy and use effective contraception during treatment
Lung damage can appear years after treatment - keep follow-up appointments lifelong
pk: Cytotoxic effect develops over days; nausea often within 2 hours
Rapidly distributed after IV; crosses blood-brain barrier within minutes
Parent drug very short (minutes); active metabolites persist longer
Marrow suppression delayed - thrombocytopenia ~4 weeks, leukopenia ~5-6 weeks after dose
Refrigerate vials at 2-8 C; protect from light
pearls: BOXED WARNING: myelosuppression is delayed and cumulative - thrombocytopenia at ~4 weeks, leukopenia at ~5-6 weeks; monitor CBC weekly for >=6 weeks and never re-dose before counts recover
BOXED WARNING: dose-related pulmonary toxicity; cumulative dose >1400 mg/m2 greatly increases risk and delayed fibrosis can be fatal years later, especially after childhood treatment
High lipid solubility lets it cross the blood-brain barrier - key for CNS tumors
Do not re-dose more often than every 6 weeks because of delayed marrow recovery
missed: Carmustine is administered in a clinical setting on a scheduled cycle. If an appointment is missed, contact the oncology team to reschedule; do not attempt to make up doses outside the prescribed every-6-week schedule.
overdose: Overdose intensifies myelosuppression (bleeding, infection), nausea, hepatotoxicity and pulmonary toxicity. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with blood product support, growth factors, infection control and monitoring of organ function.
